Weather hazards and climate change

Mission 1

Mission 1: Why are the world's rainforests and hottest deserts found in bands either side of the equator?

Make a guess: Why are the world's rainforests and hottest deserts found in bands either side of the equator?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.1 features of the global atmospheric circulation
  • 2.1 how circulation cells and ocean currents transfer and redistribute heat energy
Mission 1

Uneven heating

  • The Sun heats the Earth unevenly. Near the equator sunlight is more direct; near the poles it is spread out.
  • This sets up a temperature difference between the equator and the poles.
  • Global atmospheric circulation: the large-scale movement of air that redistributes heat and moisture around the planet.
  • Warm air moves towards the poles; cold air moves towards the equator.
Mission 1

Rising air, sinking air

  • Rising air → low pressure at the surface. It cools, clouds form, rain falls.
  • Sinking air → high pressure at the surface. It warms, clouds clear, the weather is dry.
  • At the surface, wind blows from high pressure towards low pressure.
Mission 1

The three-cell model

  • In each hemisphere, air circulates in three cells in the lowest layer of the atmosphere (up to 10–15 km high):
    • Hadley cell: equator to about 30–40°
    • Ferrel cell: about 30–40° to 60–70°
    • Polar cell: about 60–70° to the pole
  • Together they work like a "global conveyor belt" carrying energy from the tropics to the poles.
Mission 1

The pressure belts

  • Equator: low pressure. Trade winds meet and air rises in the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), forming thunderstorms.
  • About 30°: high pressure. Air from the Hadley cell sinks over the subtropics, over oceans and deserts such as the Sahara.
  • About 60°: low pressure. Warm air meets cold polar air at the polar front, "a hotspot for unsettled weather", including over the UK.
  • Poles: high pressure. Cold air sinks at the poles.
Quick check
?Why is the Sahara, at about 20–30°N, so dry?
Mission 1

Surface winds

  • Surface winds blow from the high-pressure belts to the low-pressure belts.
  • Trade winds: blow from about 30° towards the equator.
  • Westerlies: in the Ferrel cell, from the west or south-west in the northern hemisphere. They bring Atlantic weather systems to the UK.
  • Polar easterlies: blow out from the polar highs towards about 60°.
  • Coriolis effect: Earth's rotation deflects moving air to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere. So winds do not blow straight north or south.
Mission 1

Climatic zones

  • Equator (low pressure): hot, wet all year → tropical rainforests.
  • About 30° (high pressure): hot, dry → hot deserts.
  • About 60° (low pressure): mild, wet, changeable → e.g. the UK.
  • Poles (high pressure): cold and dry.
  • The circulation "shapes prevailing winds and the distribution of deserts and rainforests around the world".
Quick check
?A ship sails from the Tropic of Cancer (about 23°N) towards the equator. Which surface wind is it most likely to meet?
Mission 1

Ocean currents move heat too

  • The oceans also move heat from the equator towards the poles.
  • The Gulf Stream is "the main conveyor of heat from south to north in the Atlantic".
  • It "transports an amount of water greater than that carried by all of the world's rivers combined".
  • Deep currents form where polar water gets very cold and salty, becomes denser and sinks, starting a global "conveyer belt".
  • So heat redistribution works through two systems: circulation cells in the air and ocean currents in the sea.
Mission check

?The Amazon and Congo rainforests lie close to the equator. The Kalahari and the great Australian deserts lie close to the Tropic of Capricorn. Which explanation fits this pattern best?

Uneven heating drives the three-cell circulation. Air rises at the equator (low pressure, rain, rainforest) and sinks at about 30° (high pressure, dry, desert), so both form bands that circle the Earth.

Mission 2

Mission 2: The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined. Is that why north-west Europe has mild winters?

Make a guess: The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined. Is that why north-west Europe has mild winters?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.1 how circulation cells and ocean currents transfer and redistribute heat energy across the Earth
Mission 2

Why heat has to move

  • The tropics receive more energy from the Sun than they lose; the polar regions lose more than they receive.
  • Without a way to move heat, the tropics would keep getting hotter and the poles colder.
  • Two systems carry heat towards the poles: the atmosphere (winds and circulation cells) and the oceans (currents).
Mission 2

Surface currents and gyres

  • Wind, tides, and differences in temperature and saltiness drive ocean currents.
  • Earth's spin turns moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern: the Coriolis effect.
  • So surface currents form huge loops called gyres. There are five major ones: two in the Pacific, two in the Atlantic and one in the Indian Ocean.
Mission 2

Warm and cold currents

  • On the western side of each ocean, warm currents carry tropical water towards the poles: the Gulf Stream, the Kuroshio.
  • The Gulf Stream continues as the North Atlantic Drift towards north-west Europe.
  • On the eastern side, cold currents flow towards the equator: the Canary, the Benguela, the Humboldt.
  • Warm currents warm the air above them; cold currents cool it.
Quick check
?Which current is correctly described?
Mission 2

The Gulf Stream as a heat conveyor

  • The Gulf Stream "transports an amount of water greater than that carried by all of the world's rivers combined".
  • NOAA calls it "the main conveyor of heat from south to north in the Atlantic".
  • In cold northern waters, the ocean gives its heat to the air above: a heat transfer from ocean to atmosphere.
Mission 2

The deep conveyor belt

  • Deep currents are driven by density, which depends on temperature and salinity: the thermohaline circulation.
  • When sea ice forms, the water left behind gets saltier and denser, and sinks. Water that loses heat to the air also becomes denser and sinks.
  • NOAA describes this global ocean conveyor belt as getting its "start" in the Norwegian Sea.
  • Cold deep water flows south; warm surface water flows north to replace it, carrying heat.
Quick check
?Why does surface water sink in the far North Atlantic?
Mission 2

Does the Gulf Stream warm Europe?

  • A 2002 modelling study (Seager and others) asked why north-west Europe's winters are milder than eastern North America's at the same latitude.
  • It found that "the principal cause" is heat carried by the winds blowing off the ocean.
  • Ocean heat warms winters on both sides of the North Atlantic by "a few degC", so it cannot explain the difference between them.
  • Exam move: one model study is evidence, not proof; say what it found and weigh it.
Mission 2

A changing conveyor

  • IPCC (2021): the Atlantic part of the conveyor "is very likely to weaken over the 21st century".
  • It has "medium confidence that there will not be an abrupt collapse before 2100".
  • If it did collapse, weather patterns would very likely shift abruptly.
Mission check

?Vancouver, on Canada's west coast, has much milder winters than places at the same latitude on Asia's east coast. Using the Atlantic evidence, what is the best explanation?

Partly. Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream carry heat towards the poles and warm winters on both sides of the Atlantic by a few degrees. But Seager and others found that westerly winds off the ocean are the main reason Europe is milder than eastern North America.

Mission 3

Mission 3: How do scientists know what Earth's climate was like 800,000 years ago, long before thermometers?

Make a guess: How do scientists know what Earth's climate was like 800,000 years ago, long before thermometers?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.2 past climate change over different timescales: Quaternary glacials and interglacials
  • 2.2 natural causes (Milankovitch, solar, volcanism) and evidence (ice cores, pollen, tree rings, historical sources)
Mission 3

The Quaternary period

  • The Quaternary is the most recent period of geological time. It began 2.58 million years ago.
  • We live in its latest part, the Holocene, which began about 11,700 years ago (0.0117 million years).
  • Through the Quaternary the climate has switched again and again between cold and warm.
Mission 3

Glacials and interglacials

  • Glacials: long cold periods when ice sheets grew. Interglacials: shorter warm periods, like today.
  • In the last 800,000 years, warm interglacials came "roughly every 100,000 years".
  • At the peak of the last glacial, glaciers covered about 32% of Earth's land; today about 10%.
  • In England, ice sheets dumped the boulder clay (till) that now forms the Holderness cliffs: tills about 18,000 to 13,000 years old.
  • Smaller swings happen too: the Little Ice Age (about the early 1300s to the mid-1800s; sources date its start differently), when glaciers advanced in many areas.
Quick check
?Which statement best describes climate in the Quaternary?
Mission 3

Ice cores: how they work

  • Snow builds up in layers on ice sheets and is pressed into ice.
  • As it does, "the ice encloses small bubbles of air that contain a sample of the atmosphere". Scientists measure the CO₂ in the bubbles.
  • The ratios of different water isotopes in the ice show past temperature.
  • The oldest continuous records reach 800,000 years in Antarctica and 123,000 years in Greenland.
Mission 3

What ice cores show

  • In the ice-age cycles of the last million years or so, CO₂ "didn't get any higher than 300 ppm". Before the Industrial Revolution it was 280 ppm or less.
  • CO₂ and temperature rose and fell together through glacials and interglacials.
  • Today CO₂ is "nearly 50% higher than it was before the industrial revolution".
Quick check
?In ice cores, the fastest natural CO₂ rise is about 15 ppm in 200 years. Today CO₂ rises 15 ppm every 6 years. About how many times faster is today's rise?
Mission 3

Temperature records

  • Central England Temperature: monthly data since 1659, "the longest instrumental record of temperature in the world". It covers a triangle from Lancashire to London to Bristol.
  • Global records using thermometers start around 1850. In 2024 the world was about 1.55 °C warmer than in 1850–1900.
  • Reliability: accurate and direct, but short; early records cover few places. Since 1974, Central England data "have been adjusted to allow for urban warming".
Mission 3

Tree rings and pollen

  • Tree rings: trees grow one ring a year. Wider rings usually mean warmer or wetter growing seasons.
  • Pollen: pollen grains in lake mud and peat show which plants grew there. Warmth-loving trees mean a warmer climate.
  • Reliability: tree rings give exact years but only for the tree's lifetime and place, and growth also depends on rain, soil and disease. Pollen covers thousands of years but is dated less precisely.
Mission 3

Historical sources: diaries and paintings

  • Diaries: in Edo (Tokyo), records of cherry blossom dates and blossom-viewing parties from 1601–1905 were used to estimate March temperatures.
  • They show two cold spells (late 1600s and early 1800s), matching cold periods found in Kyoto records.
  • Paintings: show frozen rivers, snowy winters or glacier fronts at a place and time.
  • Reliability: rich local detail, but one place, not measured, and artists may exaggerate. They must be checked against other evidence.
Mission 3

Weighing the evidence

  • Ice cores: longest and continuous; a direct sample of old air. Only polar ice, and "small artefacts can arise" where the ice holds many impurities.
  • Temperature records: most accurate; only about 175 to 370 years long.
  • Sea ice: satellite-accurate since 1979; patchy before.
  • Tree rings, pollen: long or yearly; local, and affected by more than temperature.
  • Diaries, paintings: local and descriptive; need checking against measurements.
  • Scientists trust a finding most when several types agree.
Quick check
?Which source is least reliable for working out the global average temperature of the 1600s?
Mission 3

What caused the natural cycles?

  • Orbital (Milankovitch) changes: Earth's orbit, tilt and wobble change in cycles of about 100,000, 41,000 and 23,000 years. The 100,000-year beat matches the ice-core cycles.
  • Solar output: the Maunder Minimum (1645–1715), with few sunspots, fell within the Little Ice Age.
  • Volcanic eruptions: Mount Pinatubo (1991) cooled global temperature by about 0.6 °C over 15 months.
  • These are taught in full in the mission on natural causes of climate change.
Mission check

?A new Antarctic ice core is drilled. Ice from one layer, about 450,000 years old, has air bubbles with about 190 ppm of CO₂, and its water isotopes point to cold. What can scientists conclude?

Ice cores trap old air (CO₂) and record temperature in their isotopes, back 800,000 years. Scientists trust the record because ice cores, pollen, tree rings, temperature records and historical sources agree.

Mission 4

Mission 4: In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?

Make a guess: In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.2 natural causes (Milankovitch cycles, solar variation, volcanism)
Mission 4

Three natural causes

  • Earth's climate has always changed, through glacial and interglacial periods.
  • Three natural causes:
    • orbital changes (Milankovitch cycles)
    • solar output (sunspots and the solar cycle)
    • volcanic eruptions.
  • The evidence for past change (ice cores, pollen, tree rings, historical sources) is in the climate-evidence mission.
Mission 4

Milankovitch cycles

  • Eccentricity: Earth's orbit changes from more circular to more oval, in a cycle of about 100,000 years.
  • Axial tilt (obliquity): the tilt of Earth's axis changes, in about 41,000 years.
  • Precession: the axis wobbles, changing which season is nearest the Sun, about 23,000 years on average.
  • Together they change how much sunlight each latitude and season gets, pacing glacials and interglacials.
Quick check
?Why can Milankovitch cycles not explain the warming of the last 100 years?
Mission 4

Sunspots and solar output

  • Sunspots are "cooler", "darker" areas on the Sun's surface.
  • Their number rises and falls in a solar cycle of about 11 years. More sunspots go with a more active Sun.
  • Over a cycle the Sun's energy output varies by only about 0.1%.
  • The Maunder Minimum (1645–1715), "when there were few sunspots", fell within the cooler Little Ice Age, but that began centuries earlier.
  • But warming from human greenhouse gases since 1750 is "over 270 times greater" than extra warming from the Sun.
Mission 4

Volcanic eruptions: Pinatubo, 1991

  • In June 1991 Mount Pinatubo "injected about 15 million tons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere".
  • The gas formed tiny droplets (aerosols) that "scatter and absorb incoming sunlight".
  • High winds spread the haze around the world, so less sunlight reached the surface.
Mission 4

How big, and how long?

  • Global average temperature fell by about 0.6 °C over the next 15 months.
  • There was "a measurable cooling of the Earth's surface for a period of almost two years".
  • The droplets slowly fall out of the stratosphere, so the cooling fades.
  • Ash falls out within days; it is the sulfur haze that cools the whole planet.
Quick check
?Why did Pinatubo's cooling last only about two years?
Mission check

?Imagine a huge eruption injects sulfur gas high into the stratosphere. What would happen to global temperature?

Pinatubo "injected about 15 million tons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere". The haze scattered sunlight and cooled the planet by about 0.6 °C for almost two years.

Mission 5

Mission 5: The UK's emissions fell by 54% between 1990 and 2025. Has the UK really halved its part in climate change?

Make a guess: The UK's emissions fell by 54% between 1990 and 2025. Has the UK really halved its part in climate change?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.3 how industry, transport, energy and farming emit CO₂ and methane, causing the enhanced greenhouse effect
Mission 5

The natural greenhouse effect

  • Sunlight (short-wave) passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground.
  • The warm ground gives off heat (long-wave radiation).
  • Greenhouse gases (water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide) absorb some of it and give out heat in all directions, including back down.
  • Without them, Earth's surface would be about −19 °C; it averages about 14 °C.
Mission 5

The enhanced greenhouse effect

  • People add greenhouse gases faster than nature removes them.
  • More gas traps more long-wave heat, so the planet warms: the enhanced greenhouse effect.
  • 2024 levels: carbon dioxide 423.9 ppm, methane 1,942 ppb, nitrous oxide 338.0 ppb.
  • That is 52%, 166% and 25% above pre-industrial levels (before 1750).
Quick check
?What makes the greenhouse effect enhanced?
Mission 5

Cause 1: burning fossil fuels

  • Coal, oil and gas release carbon dioxide when burned.
  • In 2025 burning fossil fuels released about 38.1 billion tonnes of CO₂ (projection).
  • Energy: power stations burning coal and gas for electricity and heat.
  • Transport: petrol, diesel and jet fuel. In the UK, domestic transport made 31% of net emissions in 2025.
  • Industry: fuel for factories, plus processes such as making cement and steel.
Mission 5

Cause 2: farming

  • Cattle and sheep release methane as they digest grass. Flooded rice fields and manure release methane too.
  • Fertilisers release nitrous oxide.
  • Farming and waste together released about 228 million tonnes of methane a year (2010–2019), against 115 million tonnes from fossil fuels.
  • Methane is the second most important human-influenced greenhouse gas, after CO₂.
Quick check
?In 2025, fossil fuels released about 38.1 billion tonnes of CO₂ and land-use change (such as deforestation) about 4.1 billion tonnes. What percentage of this total came from fossil fuels, to the nearest whole number?
Mission 5

What is a carbon footprint?

  • A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas emitted to supply what a person, organisation or country uses, measured in CO₂-equivalent.
  • A country's footprint counts emissions from making its imports, wherever they happen.
  • Its territorial emissions count only what is released inside its borders.
Mission 5

The UK's footprint

  • The UK's carbon footprint was about 699 million tonnes CO₂-equivalent in 2023.
  • Emissions from making its imports rose from 31% of the footprint in 1996 to 53% in 2023.
  • Imports from China make up 25% of those import emissions.
Mission 5

Two measures, two stories

  • Since 1996, the UK's territorial emissions fell by 50%; its carbon footprint by only 15%.
  • Defra links this to "a shift from manufacturing towards a service-based economy, alongside an increased reliance on imported goods and services".
  • Some cuts were real: the UK's last coal power station closed in September 2024.
Quick check
?Why has the UK's carbon footprint fallen much less than its territorial emissions?
Mission check

?A country's territorial emissions fell by 40% over 20 years. In the same years it closed its steelworks and began importing most of its steel and electronics. Has its part in climate change fallen by 40%?

The UK's territorial emissions halved, but its carbon footprint fell by only 15% (1996–2023), because 53% of the footprint now comes from imports. Part of the cut is real; part has moved abroad.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Global sea level has risen about 10 cm since 1993, and the yearly rise has more than doubled. Where is the extra water coming from?

Make a guess: Global sea level has risen about 10 cm since 1993, and the yearly rise has more than doubled. Where is the extra water coming from?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.3 negative effects on environment and people: changing crop yields, rising sea levels, retreating glaciers
Mission 6

The sea is rising faster

  • Global sea level rose 0.20 m between 1901 and 2018.
  • The yearly rise sped up: 1.3 mm a year (1901–1971), 1.9 mm (1971–2006), 3.7 mm (2006–2018).
  • Satellites: about 10 cm since 1993.
Mission 6

Where the extra water comes from

  • Thermal expansion: seawater takes up more space as it warms.
  • Melting land ice: water from glaciers and ice sheets runs into the sea.
  • Shares of the rise, 1971–2018: thermal expansion 50%, glaciers 22%, ice sheets 20%, other land water 8%.
  • Melting sea ice adds almost nothing: it is already floating, so it already displaces its own weight of water.
Quick check
?Which of these adds least to sea-level rise?
Mission 6

Retreating glaciers

  • Reference glaciers worldwide lost on average 214 mm of water-equivalent thickness per decade in the 1980s, and 896 mm per decade in the 2010s.
  • Glacier National Park, USA: about 80 glaciers larger than 0.1 km² around 1850; 32 in 2005.
  • People: in the upper Indus basin, glacier melt made up 40.6% of river runoff (1998–2007). Shrinking glaciers threaten that water supply in the long term.
Mission 6

Effects on the environment

  • About half of the species studied worldwide have moved towards the poles or uphill.
  • From early 2023 to mid-2025, heat stress able to bleach coral hit 84% of the world's reef area.
  • Climate zones are shifting: dry (arid) zones are expanding and polar zones shrinking.
Mission 6

Effects on people

  • Health: heat-related deaths average 546,000 a year, a rate 23% higher than in the 1990s.
  • Diseases carried by mosquitoes and ticks have spread to new areas.
  • Displacement: storms forced 17.9 million movements in 2025. Not every disaster is caused by climate change; scientists test each event.
  • About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in places highly vulnerable to climate change.
Quick check
?Which is an effect of climate change on people, rather than on the environment?
Mission 6

Food: changing crop yields

  • Farm output keeps growing, but climate change "has slowed this growth over the past 50 years globally".
  • Losers: yields of some crops, such as maize and wheat, have fallen in many lower-latitude (tropical) regions.
  • Winners: some crops (maize, wheat, sugar beet) have gained in many higher-latitude regions.
  • In Africa, livestock on pasture grow more slowly.
Mission 6

Predicted sea level

  • By 2100, compared with 1995–2014: a likely rise of 0.28–0.55 m if emissions are very low, and 0.63–1.01 m if they are very high.
  • These are projections: the range depends on how much people emit.
Quick check
?Which statement about climate change and crop yields is best supported?
Mission check

?Imagine two summers. In summer 1, 100 billion tonnes of floating Arctic sea ice melts. In summer 2, 100 billion tonnes of ice melts from Greenland's ice sheet on land, and the upper ocean warms. Which summer raises sea level more?

The extra water comes from melting land ice (glaciers and ice sheets) and from thermal expansion of warming seawater, which explained half the rise in 1971–2018. Rising seas are one of many effects on people, places and the economy.

Mission 7

Mission 7: The wettest Scottish mountains get about eight times the rain of the driest parts of eastern England. Why?

Make a guess: The wettest Scottish mountains get about eight times the rain of the driest parts of eastern England. Why?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.4 UK climate today and its changes over the last 1000 years
  • 2.4 spatial variation in UK temperature, prevailing wind and rainfall
  • 2.4 significance of the UK's geographic location for its climate
Mission 7

Weather or climate?

  • Weather: the state of the atmosphere at one place and time: today's rain, wind, temperature.
  • Climate: "the general weather over a long period", usually averaged over 30 years.
  • One cold week is weather. Thirty years of average temperatures is climate.
Mission 7

The UK's climate today

  • Temperate maritime: mild, wet, changeable, with no dry season.
  • Mean annual temperature: about 7 °C in Shetland to over 11 °C in the far south-west of England.
  • Annual rainfall: over 4,000 mm in the western Scottish mountains; around 500 mm in the driest parts of eastern England.
  • "Places in the east and south of the UK tend to be drier, warmer, sunnier and less windy than those further west and north".
Mission 7

Latitude

  • Further north, the Sun is lower in the sky, so its energy is spread over a larger area: colder.
  • So mean annual temperatures fall from over 11 °C in the far south-west to about 7 °C in Shetland.
  • North–south: temperature. West–east: rainfall (see prevailing winds, coming up).
Mission 7

Altitude

  • Temperature falls by about 0.5 °C for every 100 m of height.
  • Moist air forced up hills cools, condenses and makes cloud and rain: relief rainfall.
  • So a map of rainfall "looks very similar to a topographic map".
Mission 7

Prevailing wind and the Atlantic

  • The UK's prevailing winds are west to south-westerly, blowing in off the Atlantic.
  • They bring moist air and Atlantic depressions, which give most of the autumn and winter rain.
  • The air meets the western mountains first and drops its rain there. The east lies in a rain shadow.
  • Exam move: explain spatial variation by linking a factor (wind, relief) to a place and a figure.
Quick check
?Why does the west of the UK get much more rain than the east?
Mission 7

Ocean currents: the North Atlantic Drift

  • The Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Drift, carry warm water from the tropics towards north-west Europe.
  • The Met Office notes that the warm Gulf Stream has "a strong influence" on western Scotland.
  • Winds blowing off this warm ocean keep UK winters mild for their latitude. Most of that warmth arrives through the winds; the ocean current adds "a few °C" in winter.
Mission 7

Maritime and continental climates

  • The sea heats up and cools down slowly; land does both quickly.
  • Maritime: near the sea, small yearly temperature range. About 9 °C in the Hebrides, the gap between the warmest and coldest month.
  • More continental: further from the sea, bigger range. About 14 °C in the English Midlands.
  • Winds from mainland Europe bring continental extremes: hot summer days on south-easterly winds, and the coldest winter spells when "a strong, cold easterly wind ousts the normal south westerlies".
Quick check
?In February, cold dry air arrives over England on an easterly wind. Where has this air most likely come from?
Mission 7

1,000 years of change

  • Medieval Warm Period (about 1,000 years ago): some regions were as warm as today, but the world as a whole was "well below recent levels".
  • Little Ice Age: coldest from about 1400 to 1700, with the greatest cooling over northern continents.
  • Both swings were responses to natural changes. The coldest part included the Maunder Minimum (1645–1715), when there were few sunspots.
  • Today's warming is different: since 1750, warming from human greenhouse gases has been over 270 times the extra warming from the Sun.
Mission 7

The evidence: Central England Temperature

  • The Central England Temperature series starts in 1659: "the longest instrumental record of temperature in the world".
  • Coldest decade: the 1690s, average 8.13 °C (our calculation).
  • Coldest year: 1740, at 6.86 °C. Warmest: 2025, at 11.23 °C.
  • 2016–2025 averaged 10.80 °C (our calculation).
Quick check
?The 1690s averaged 8.13 °C in central England; 2016–2025 averaged 10.80 °C. How much warmer was the recent decade?
Mission check

?Town A is on a west coast at sea level, facing prevailing winds off a warm ocean. Town B is at the same latitude and height, but far inland to the east, beyond a range of mountains. Compared with Town B, Town A is most likely to be:

In the UK, westerly winds off the Atlantic drop their rain on the western mountains (over 4,000 mm a year) and leave eastern England in a rain shadow (around 500 mm). The sea also keeps the west's temperature range small: about 9 °C in the Hebrides, 14 °C in the Midlands.

Mission 8

Mission 8: Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?

Make a guess: Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.5 how global circulation leads to tropical cyclones in source areas, and the formation sequence
  • 2.5 characteristics, frequency and distribution, and how these change over time
  • 2.6 why tropical cyclones are hazards (high winds, intense rain, storm surge, coastal flooding, landslides)
Mission 8

One storm, three names

  • A tropical cyclone is "a rapidly rotating storm that begins over tropical oceans".
  • It is called a hurricane in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, a typhoon in the north-west Pacific, and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.
Mission 8

Where and when

  • They form over tropical oceans, between about 25°S and 25°N.
  • They do not form within about 480 km (300 miles) of the equator: there is too little spin there.
  • Main seasons: July–October in the Northern Hemisphere, December–March in the Southern; globally, September is the most active month.
  • The north-west Pacific has them all year round. Over cool water or land, they weaken.
Mission 8

Linked to global circulation

  • Near the equator, the trade winds of the two Hadley cells meet. Warm air rises: a belt of low pressure and thunderstorms.
  • Tropical storms grow from disturbances in this rising air over warm oceans: the source areas.
  • Trade winds then steer most storms westwards; many later curve towards the poles.
Quick check
?Why do tropical storms almost never form right on the equator, even where the sea is warm?
Mission 8

The ingredients

  • Warm ocean: about 27 °C (80 °F) at the surface, and warm down to about 46 m (150 feet).
  • Moist air high up, and air that cools quickly with height.
  • Low wind shear: winds at different heights must be similar, so the storm is not torn apart.
  • Spin from the Coriolis force, so at least about 480 km (300 miles) from the equator.
  • A pre-existing disturbance: an area of low pressure with thunderstorms. Even with all of these, many disturbances never develop.
Mission 8

How one forms: the sequence

  • 1. Warm sea heats the air above it, and lots of water evaporates.
  • 2. Moist air rises, cools and condenses into huge clouds. Condensation releases latent heat, which warms the air so it rises faster.
  • 3. Air pressure at the surface falls; more air rushes in to replace the rising air.
  • 4. The Coriolis force makes the in-rushing air spiral; thunderstorms organise into a rotating storm.
  • 5. Over land or cold water, the supply of warm, moist air is cut off and the storm weakens.
Mission 8

Structure

  • Eye: the calm centre, with the lowest pressure; air sinks, so skies are often clear.
  • Eyewall: a ring of towering clouds round the eye, with the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
  • Rain bands: spiral bands of cloud and rain further out.
  • Air spirals in near the surface, rises in the eyewall and flows out at the top.
Quick check
?Where does a tropical storm get most of the energy that keeps it going?
Mission 8

Measuring strength: the Saffir–Simpson scale

  • Hurricanes are rated 1 to 5 by their maximum sustained wind:
  • Category 1: 74–95 mph (64–82 kt) · Category 2: 96–110 mph (83–95 kt) · Category 3: 111–129 mph (96–112 kt) · Category 4: 130–156 mph (113–136 kt) · Category 5: 157 mph or more (137 kt or more).
  • Categories 3–5 are major hurricanes.
  • The scale "does not take into account" storm surge, rainfall flooding or tornadoes.
Quick check
?Hurricane Ian made landfall in Florida with winds of 130 knots. Which category was it?
Mission 8

Why tropical storms are hazards

  • High winds destroy buildings, trees and power lines and turn debris into missiles.
  • Intense rain causes river and flash flooding inland.
  • Storm surge: "an abnormal water level rise generated by a storm" above the normal tide, driven mainly by strong onshore winds. It is highest where the sea floor slopes gently. It causes coastal flooding.
  • Landslides: rain soaks steep slopes. Hurricane Maria (2017) triggered more than 40,000 landslides in Puerto Rico.
Mission 8

Hurricane Ian, 2022: Florida

  • Ian intensified rapidly over water of 30 °C and above, with low wind shear (winds at different heights were similar).
  • 28 September: it peaked at 140 kt (category 5), then hit Cayo Costa, Florida, at 130 kt (category 4).
  • Storm surge (sea water piled up by onshore winds) flooded Fort Myers Beach to 3–4.6 m (10–15 feet) above ground.
  • In Lee County, at least 52,514 buildings were damaged, 5,369 of them destroyed.
  • At least 156 people died in the US, 66 directly from the storm: surge killed 41, freshwater flooding 12 and wind 4.
Quick check
?Of Ian's 66 direct deaths in the US, 41 were caused by storm surge. What percentage is that, to the nearest whole number?
Mission 8

Are tropical storms changing?

  • Intensity: the share of storms reaching the strongest categories (3–5) has likely risen over the last four decades.
  • Distribution: in the north-west Pacific, the place where storms reach their peak has very likely moved further north.
  • Frequency: scientists have "low confidence" in long-term trends in the total number of storms.
  • Rain: human-caused warming increases the heavy rain they bring (high confidence).
  • Future: the share of the most intense storms (categories 4–5) and their top wind speeds are projected to rise as the world warms (high confidence).
Quick check
?Which statement best matches the IPCC's findings on tropical storms?
Mission check

?A category 3 hurricane is heading for a low-lying coast with a wide, gently sloping sea floor and a bay that narrows inland. Which hazard is likely to kill most people?

Ian's onshore winds drove a storm surge 3–4.6 m (10–15 feet) above ground at Fort Myers Beach. Surge caused 41 of the 66 direct deaths in the US (62%); wind caused 4.

Mission 9

Mission 9: A hurricane hit Cuba, then Florida. The USA is far richer than Cuba, so why did far more people die in Florida?

Make a guess: A hurricane hit Cuba, then Florida. The USA is far richer than Cuba, so why did far more people die in Florida?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.6 social, economic and environmental impacts in a named developed and a named emerging/developing country
  • 2.6 responses of individuals, organisations and governments in both
Mission 9

Hurricane Ian, 2022

  • 27 Sept: hit western Cuba (Pinar del Río) as a category 3 hurricane, 110 kt.
  • It strengthened again over the sea, then hit south-west Florida on 28 Sept as a category 4, 130 kt.
  • Income per person (GNI per capita, 2021 PPP $): USA about $73,650; Cuba about $8,415, a UN estimate.
  • USA: very high HDI (0.938) = developed. Cuba: high HDI (0.762) = emerging.
Mission 9

Primary effects: Florida

  • Primary effects are caused directly by the wind, rain and sea.
  • Storm surge flooded Fort Myers Beach 3–4.6 m (10–15 ft) above ground.
  • Lee County: at least 52,514 buildings damaged; 5,369 destroyed.
  • Roads and bridges to Sanibel and Pine Islands were washed away; they could be reached only by boat or helicopter.
  • 66 direct deaths in the US, all in Florida; storm surge killed 41.
Mission 9

Secondary effects: Florida

  • Secondary effects follow on from the primary ones.
  • About 4.45 million customers (about 9.62 million people) lost power in the US.
  • 90 more deaths were indirect: lack of timely medical care (18), falls and other accidents during power cuts (16), heart attacks (16).
  • Floodwater carried debris, fertiliser and pollutants into the sea; scientists then tracked a harmful algal bloom.
  • Crop and farm losses in Florida: $1.1–1.8 billion. Total US damage: $112.9 billion.
Mission 9

Effects in Cuba

  • Storm surge pushed the sea 300 m inland at La Coloma.
  • More than 100,000 homes damaged or destroyed; the whole island lost power for a few days.
  • 5 deaths, 3 of them direct.
  • Tobacco, a key export (10.4% of goods exports) and a main livelihood in Pinar del Río, suffered "disastrous" losses, putting the next harvest at risk.
  • More than 70 schools in Pinar del Río were damaged.
  • No dollar estimate of Cuba's losses exists, so the two cannot be compared in money.
Quick check
?Which of these was a secondary effect of Hurricane Ian?
Mission 9

Shorter-term and longer-term impacts

  • Shorter term (days to weeks): deaths, flooding, power cuts (Cuba's two worst-hit provinces were still without power two days later), water rescues: over 250 in central and eastern Florida.
  • Longer term (months to years): rebuilding homes; lost tobacco harvest; Florida's federal recovery support passing $10.2 billion two years on.
  • Social: deaths, homes, schools · Economic: $112.9 bn US damage, crops, tobacco · Environmental: algal bloom, damaged artificial reefs.
Quick check
?Which impact of Ian on Cuba was longer term?
Mission 9

Immediate responses

  • Warnings: the US National Hurricane Center briefed emergency managers from 23 Sept, as Ian formed.
  • Florida: a storm surge watch, then a warning, were issued for Fort Myers Beach 48 h and 30 h before tropical-storm winds arrived.
  • Cuba: Civil Defence moved 76,221 people out of danger, to government shelters or to friends and family.
  • Rescue: over 250 water rescues in Florida; the US Coast Guard received 16 live briefings from the NHC to support its rescues.
Mission 9

Long-term responses

  • USA: federal support passed $10.2 billion within two years.
  • $1.15 billion went to 387,139 households; flood insurance paid $4.67 billion to about 47,000 policyholders.
  • Cuba: the Red Cross appealed for 9 million Swiss francs to help 25,000 people, but received only 43% of it.
  • Many Cuban families rebuilt with salvaged materials; the Red Cross called for sturdier, longer-lasting shelter.
Mission 9

Who responded?

  • Individuals: left their homes when told to; Cuban families sheltered relatives and rebuilt their own homes.
  • Organisations: the Cuban Red Cross with the IFRC; UN agencies in Cuba; the US Coast Guard.
  • Governments: Cuba's Civil Defence ran the evacuation; the US federal government (FEMA) paid for recovery.
  • Cuba is cut off from major international lenders, which made paying for recovery harder.
Quick check
?Which response to Ian was long term?
Quick check
?Florida had far more money than Cuba, yet more people died there. Which reason is best supported by the evidence?
Mission check

?Two coasts are hit by equally strong cyclones. Coast X is wealthy, with good forecasts, but many people choose to stay in low-lying homes. Coast Y is poorer, but its civil defence moves everyone from low-lying areas to shelters before the storm. Which statement is most likely?

Cuba evacuated 76,221 people and lost 5 lives, but recovery money was short (43% of the Red Cross appeal). Florida had $10.2 billion of federal support, yet Ian hit it harder, at 130 kt, and 41 people drowned in the storm surge.

Mission 10

Mission 10: In June 2021 a Canadian village reached 49.6 °C, a national record. Could that have happened without climate change?

Make a guess: In June 2021 a Canadian village reached 49.6 °C, a national record. Could that have happened without climate change?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.7 characteristics of arid environments compared with the extreme weather of drought
  • 2.7 causes of drought: meteorological, hydrological, human (agriculture, dam building, deforestation)
  • 2.7 why global circulation makes some places more drought-vulnerable, and how this changes over time
Mission 10

High pressure: sinking air

  • In an anticyclone (high pressure), air sinks and warms as it falls.
  • Sinking air stops clouds forming: clear skies, strong sunshine, little rain.
  • If a high stalls for days (a blocking high), heat builds day after day: a heatwave.
  • If highs keep returning for months, rain fails: drought.
Mission 10

Why some places are more at risk

  • At the equator, air rises: low pressure and heavy rain.
  • Around 30° north and south, that air sinks: belts of high pressure. Many of the world's hot deserts lie here.
  • The rain belt moves north and south with the seasons. Places at its edge, such as the Sahel, depend on a short rainy season that can fail.
  • Heatwaves can strike much further from the equator too, wherever a blocking high stalls in summer.
Mission 10

Arid is not the same as drought

  • Arid: a climate that is always dry. Scientists use an aridity index: rainfall ÷ the water the air could evaporate. Arid areas score 0.05–0.20; hyper-arid below 0.05.
  • Drought: a temporary spell of below-normal water for that place. It can hit wet places as well as dry ones.
  • Drylands (arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid) cover about 46.2% of the world's land and are home to about 3 billion people.
Quick check
?Which describes a drought rather than an arid environment?
Mission 10

Causes of drought

  • Meteorological: much less rain than normal, often under persistent high pressure.
  • Hydrological: rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater fall low, often months after the rain fails.
  • Human: agriculture: pumping too much water for irrigation drains rivers and aquifers.
  • Human: dam building: a dam upstream holds back water, so less reaches people downstream.
  • Human: deforestation: fewer trees return less moisture to the air, and bare soil dries faster.
  • Higher temperatures add to all of these by raising evaporation.
Mission 10

Changing over time: the Sahel

  • Sahel summer rainfall was high in the 1950s and 1960s, fell sharply in the 1970s and 1980s (driest year in the index: 1984), and has partly recovered since 1990.
  • The IPCC links a cooler North Atlantic to a drier Sahel; air pollution (aerosols) has also been suggested as a cause of the droughts.
  • Worldwide, dry (arid) climate zones have expanded. A farming drought that came once in 10 years in drying regions now comes 1.7 times per decade.
Quick check
?Why is the Sahel more vulnerable to drought than places on the equator?
Mission 10

Heatwaves are changing

  • IPCC: it is "virtually certain" that heatwaves have become more frequent and more intense over most land regions since the 1950s.
  • A heat extreme that used to come once in 10 years now comes 2.8 times per decade.
  • At 2 °C of warming it is projected to come 5.6 times per decade.
Mission 10

Case study: the Pacific Northwest heatwave, June 2021

  • Where: western Canada (British Columbia) and the north-west USA.
  • Cause: "a slow-moving strong high pressure system", sometimes called a heat dome, which reached record strength.
  • Sinking air and winds blowing down the mountainsides heated the air further.
  • In British Columbia temperatures rose from 24 June to a peak on 28–29 June, passing 40 °C in many places.
  • Lytton set Canada's all-time record: 49.6 °C.
Mission 10

Could it happen without climate change?

  • Attribution science compares how likely an event is today with a modelled world without human-caused warming.
  • World Weather Attribution: the heatwave was "virtually impossible without human-caused climate change".
  • An event this rare would have been at least 150 times rarer without it, and the heat was about 2 °C hotter.
  • The heat dome itself is weather. Climate change made its heat more extreme.
Mission check

?A city has its hottest day ever, during a stalled high-pressure system. Which statement could an attribution study support?

For Lytton, World Weather Attribution found the heat "virtually impossible without human-caused climate change": about 2 °C hotter, and at least 150 times more likely. The heat dome was weather; warming made it deadlier.

Mission 11

Mission 11: California and Ethiopia both had years of drought. Why were the results so different?

Make a guess: California and Ethiopia both had years of drought. Why were the results so different?

Specification: what this mission covers

Edexcel GCSE Geography A (1GA0)

  • 2.8 reasons why droughts are hazardous
  • 2.8 how drought impacts on people and ecosystems vary between a named developed and a named emerging/developing country
  • 2.8 responses to drought by individuals, organisations and governments in a named developed and a named emerging/developing country
Mission 11

Why droughts are hazardous

  • Slow onset: a drought creeps up; it is hard to say when it starts or ends.
  • Long duration: it can last for years. "As drought persists, longer-term impacts can emerge, such as land subsidence, seawater intrusion, and damage to ecosystems".
  • Wide area: whole regions or countries are affected at once.
  • Many impacts: water supply, food, farm income, health, wildlife, wildfire.
  • Hard to plan for: the long duration of the 2020–23 Horn of Africa drought "raises serious questions about the length of droughts that government drought management systems and the international aid infrastructure should be prepared to handle".
Quick check
?Which feature makes drought different from most other weather hazards?
Mission 11

Two named countries

Edexcel groups countries by the Human Development Index (HDI):

  • USA: HDI 0.938, "very high" → developed (2023 values).
  • Ethiopia: HDI 0.497, "low" → developing.
  • Case studies: California, USA, 2012–16 and Ethiopia, in the Horn of Africa drought, 2020–23.
Mission 11

California 2012–16: impacts on people

  • "One of the most severe droughts on record".
  • River water for Central Valley farms was cut by about one-third in 2014.
  • 2014: about 17,100 farm jobs lost and 428,000 acres of cropland left unplanted.
  • Over the drought, farm losses of nearly $2 billion; more than 2,000 household wells ran dry.
  • Food prices for shoppers were "largely unaffected".
Mission 11

California: impacts on ecosystems

  • As many as 18 fish species, including most salmon and steelhead runs, were "at risk of extinction if the drought continues".
  • Wildlife refuges for migratory birds "faced shortfalls" of water.
  • Giant sequoias in Sequoia and Kings Canyon national parks lost water from their foliage, and a few died.
  • Dry, dense forests were at greater risk of extreme wildfire.
Mission 11

Ethiopia 2020–23: impacts on people

  • From late 2020, southern Ethiopia, southern Somalia and eastern Kenya had five failed rainy seasons in a row.
  • April 2022: more than 8 million people affected in southern and south-eastern Ethiopia.
  • Across Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia, about 22 million people were "acutely food insecure" because of the drought (2023).
  • 1.75 million people were internally displaced in Ethiopia and Somalia by January 2023.
Mission 11

Ethiopia: impacts on ecosystems and livestock

  • Poor rains left "below-normal pasture and water availability", cutting milk production.
  • More than 4.5 million livestock died from late 2021, with a further 30 million "weakened and emaciated".
  • Herders lose their main source of food and income when pasture and animals die.
Quick check
?Which statement best compares the impacts?
Mission 11

Why the impacts differed

  • California: farms fell back on groundwater. "California's agricultural economy overall is doing remarkably well, thanks mostly to groundwater reserves" (2014).
  • Ethiopia: many households depend on rain-fed farming and herding, the groups most "vulnerable to drought".
  • Wealth: money for wells, pumps, insurance and imported food.
  • Development (HDI) affects how well people can cope, not how much rain falls.
Mission 11

California: who responded?

  • Individuals: under the state mandate, households and businesses cut use; urban areas used nearly 25% less water between 2013 and early 2016. Farmers pumped more groundwater and left fields unplanted.
  • Organisations: university researchers (UC Davis) measured the impacts for the state's farm department.
  • Government: a statewide water conservation mandate in April 2015; the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act, 2014, to stop groundwater being used up.
Mission 11

Ethiopia: who responded?

  • Individuals: herders moved animals to find pasture; some people migrated. One in four migrants leaving or returning to Ethiopia came from drought-affected regions.
  • Organisations: the World Food Programme gave food and cash, reaching over 8.8 million people a month across the Horn of Africa. IOM appealed for $59 million to help 2.5 million people in Ethiopia.
  • Government: Ethiopia's Productive Safety Net Programme, backed by World Bank funding approved in 2004, gives poor rural households predictable support instead of emergency relief. It is designed to scale up in a crisis.
Quick check
?Which is a response by a government?
Mission check

?In the same dry year, a wheat farmer in Australia (very high HDI) and a camel herder in Somalia (low HDI) both get very little rain. Which explanation of the different impacts is best?

Drought hits rich and poor places alike, but wealth buys buffers: stored water and groundwater, savings, insurance and strong government support. In California the losses were mostly money and jobs; in Ethiopia millions of people went hungry and millions of animals died.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Uneven heating → three cells (Hadley, Ferrel, Polar) → belts of low pressure (equator, about 60°) and high pressure (about 30°, poles) → surface winds (trade winds, westerlies) bent by the Coriolis effect.
  • Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream also carry heat towards the poles.

Mission 2

  • Ocean currents redistribute heat: warm currents carry it poleward on the western sides of oceans, and the thermohaline conveyor links the oceans at depth.
  • North-west Europe's mild winters come partly from ocean heat, carried ashore mainly by the westerly winds.

Mission 3

  • The Quaternary (2.58 million years to today) has cycled between glacials and interglacials; CO₂ now is about 50% above pre-industrial levels.
  • Evidence: ice cores (CO₂ and temperature, 800,000 years), temperature records (since 1659 in England), sea ice (satellites since 1979), tree rings, pollen, diaries and paintings. Each has limits; agreement between them gives confidence.

Mission 4

  • Natural causes: Milankovitch cycles (100,000, 41,000, 23,000 years), sunspots (11-year cycle, ~0.1% change), volcanoes (Pinatubo: −0.6 °C, about two years).

Mission 5

  • Fossil fuels, farming and deforestation add CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide faster than nature removes them: the enhanced greenhouse effect.
  • A carbon footprint counts emissions from everything consumed, including imports. The UK's fell far less than its territorial emissions.
  • Link each sector to its gas: energy, transport and industry (CO₂); farming (methane, nitrous oxide).

Mission 6

  • Sea level rises because seawater expands as it warms and land ice melts.
  • Effects reach the environment (species, coral, glaciers) and people (heat, disease, displacement).

Mission 7

  • Weather is day to day; climate is the 30-year average. The UK's climate is temperate maritime.
  • Latitude makes the north cooler; altitude makes hills cooler and wetter; south-westerly winds off the Atlantic and the North Atlantic Drift make the west wet and mild; continental air from Europe brings hot summer days and cold winter spells.
  • Central England has warmed from 8.13 °C in the 1690s (Little Ice Age) to 10.80 °C in 2016–2025.

Mission 8

  • Tropical storms form over oceans warmer than about 27 °C, away from the equator, where low pressure, low wind shear and Coriolis spin let thunderstorms organise. Latent heat drives them.
  • A larger share now reach the strongest categories; their total number shows no clear trend.
  • On low coasts, storm surge is usually the deadliest hazard: in Ian, 41 of 66 direct US deaths.

Mission 9

  • Primary effects come from the storm itself (surge, wind, rain); secondary effects follow (power cuts, lost harvests, indirect deaths).
  • Immediate responses save lives (warnings, evacuation, rescue); long-term responses rebuild (aid, insurance, reconstruction). Wealth speeds recovery more than it prevents deaths.

Mission 10

  • Sinking air in high pressure brings clear skies and little rain: heatwaves and droughts.
  • High-pressure belts near 30° and the edges of the seasonal rain belt (the Sahel) are most at risk; the Sahel dried in the 1970s–80s and has partly recovered.
  • Arid = always dry; drought = temporary shortage. Causes: meteorological, hydrological and human.
  • Pacific Northwest, June 2021: a heat dome; 619 deaths in British Columbia. Warming made it about 2 °C hotter.

Mission 11

  • Drought is hazardous because it is slow, long, widespread and hard to plan for.
  • California 2012–16 (USA, very high HDI): job and farm losses, dry wells, salmon and forests at risk; responses included water cuts, groundwater pumping and new laws.
  • Ethiopia 2020–23 (low HDI): millions hungry, more than 4.5 million livestock dead; responses from herders, WFP, IOM and the government's safety net.
  • The difference lies in vulnerability and capacity to cope, not only in the rainfall.
